name: Old Dominion Line / Pier 26 Waterfront
address: Pier 26 Tide Deck, Hudson River Park, New York, NY
intro: In autumn 1907, nineteen-year-old Georgia O’Keeffe arrived in Manhattan by boat. Her likely route took her from Virginia aboard an Old Dominion Line passenger steamer bound for Pier 26 on the Hudson River. She expected her brother to meet her, but neither he nor the friend he had deputized appeared. An older woman she met aboard the boat helped her navigate the unfamiliar city.
readmore: Contemporary advertisements document the Old Dominion Line’s evening departures from Norfolk for New York. O’Keeffe’s precise sailing and vessel remain unknown.

In her recollection “My First Trip to New York,” transcribed in 1983, she remembered the helpful stranger, the streetcars and finding the unfamiliar address where she would live. Her Manhattan story began not in a gallery, but with a journey through its streets.

name: 291 — Alfred Stieglitz’s Gallery
intro: On a snowy January day in 1908, Georgia O’Keeffe and several fellow Art Students League students walked south to Alfred Stieglitz’s small gallery at 291 Fifth Avenue. They had come to see drawings by Auguste Rodin. Eight years later, Stieglitz would exhibit O’Keeffe’s own drawings in these rooms—without first asking her permission.
readmore: “It was a day with snow on everything,” O’Keeffe remembered of her first visit. The Rodin drawings were unlike anything she had been taught to make.

On January 1, 1916, her friend Anita Pollitzer brought O’Keeffe’s abstract charcoals to Stieglitz. Their correspondence began. When he exhibited ten drawings that May, O’Keeffe confronted him: “Who gave you permission to hang these drawings?”

In April 1917, 291 presented her first solo exhibition. She was teaching in Texas during most of its public run. Stieglitz later rehung the work so she could see it and photographed her beside her watercolor Blue I. The gallery closed that year.

name: American Radiator Building
intro: In Radiator Building—Night, New York (1927), Georgia O’Keeffe painted the black-and-gold tower at 40 West 40th Street beneath sweeping beams of light. On the neighboring building, a real sign advertised the magazine “Scientific American.” O’Keeffe replaced that advertisement with “Alfred Stieglitz” in glowing red letters. The man who had photographed and exhibited her work appeared, this time, in a city painting that she composed herself.
readmore: The American Radiator Building still stands at 40 West 40th Street. Visitors can compare its dark facade and gold crown with O’Keeffe’s painted version.

Searchlights open above the dark tower, while illuminated windows punctuate its facade. O’Keeffe retained enough of the building to make it recognizable, but rearranged the city’s lights and signs to make a painting of her own.

name: Hotel Chatham — New York Street with Moon
address: Vanderbilt Avenue (former alignment), between East 48th and East 49th Streets, Manhattan, New York, NY — approximate historic site
intro: Georgia O’Keeffe’s New York Street with Moon (1925) looks upward between tall buildings toward a small patch of night sky. The High Museum associates the setting with streets near the Hotel Chatham. O’Keeffe was beginning to paint Manhattan not as a precise street map, but as the experience of looking up through a canyon of buildings. The moon, streetlamp and high walls become the essential elements of the scene.
readmore: In 1926 O’Keeffe explained: “One can’t paint New York as it is, but rather as it is felt.”
A period colorized postcard of the Hotel Chatham on East 48th Street shows a comparable street view, including a gooseneck streetlight on the corner.
The historic postcard provides a comparable period street view, not proof of the precise position from which O’Keeffe painted.

name: Waldorf Astoria — Chrysler Building view
intro: Around 1960, more than a decade after making New Mexico her permanent home, Georgia O’Keeffe photographed the Chrysler Building through a window at the Waldorf Astoria. A pale curtain frames the tower, holding the hotel room and the skyline in the same image. Earlier she had painted New York from the high rooms she shared with Alfred Stieglitz at the Shelton Hotel. Now, returning to Manhattan as a visitor, she looked at the city through her own camera.
readmore: The Waldorf Astoria’s building survives at 301 Park Avenue.

name: Beverly Hotel — New York, Night
intro: O’Keeffe’s narrow, glowing painting New York, Night (1928–1929) looks north toward the Beverly Hotel on East 50th Street from their home at the Shelton Hotel. At night, Lexington Avenue appeared to her like a “very tall thin bottle,” alive with colored movement. Against deep darkness she concentrated electric lights and the vertical forms of the buildings. Alfred Stieglitz photographed a comparable view north from Room 3003 at the Shelton in 1927, making a revealing companion to O’Keeffe’s painted interpretation.
readmore: The two artists looked toward much the same city. Stieglitz recorded the illuminated buildings from his window; O’Keeffe concentrated their lights and vertical forms into a narrow shaft of color against the darkness.

name: Downtown Gallery — The 1961 Exhibition
address: 32 East 51st Street, between Madison and Park Avenues, New York, NY 10022
intro: From April 11 to May 6, 1961, Edith Halpert’s Downtown Gallery at 32 East 51st Street presented Georgia O’Keeffe’s Recent Paintings and Drawings. Halpert had become her New York dealer after An American Place closed in 1950. O’Keeffe had made New Mexico her permanent home in 1949, but her paintings continued to return to Manhattan. Her first solo exhibition had been held at 291 in 1917; forty-four years later, she was still showing new work in the city where her career had developed.
readmore: In October 1950, O’Keeffe returned to New York to install Georgia O’Keeffe: Paintings 1946–1950, the final exhibition at An American Place.
That December, O’Keeffe instructed Doris Bry to send most of the paintings still stored in the city to New Mexico. Yet her relationship with Manhattan’s galleries continued.

name: Radio City Music Hall — A Mural Unrealized
address: 1260 Avenue of the Americas, New York, NY
intro: In April 1932, Georgia O’Keeffe accepted a $1,500 commission to paint floral decoration for the women’s second-mezzanine powder room at the new Radio City Music Hall. She had not consulted Alfred Stieglitz before accepting it. He opposed the project, but she proceeded. When she visited the site with designer Donald Deskey, prepared canvas had begun detaching from the wall plaster. Delays mounted as the theater’s opening approached. O’Keeffe did not complete the mural. Yasuo Kuniyoshi supplied the botanical decoration now visible in the restored room.
readmore: O’Keeffe had accepted the commission without consulting Stieglitz. But delays in preparing the room prevented her from beginning the mural as planned. By the end of 1932, the commission had collapsed and she had stopped painting.

Writing decades later, Donald Deskey remembered O’Keeffe’s response: “O’Keeffe became hysterical and left in tears.  The next day, Stieglitz telephoned to say that she had had a nervous breakdown, was confined to a sanitorium and hence would be unable to fulfill her contract.”
The botanical decoration by Yasuo Kuniyoshi survives in the restored room—a reminder of the work O’Keeffe had intended to make here.

name: N. W. Ayer / Dole — Rockefeller Center
intro: Through the advertising agency N. W. Ayer, the Hawaiian Pineapple Company approached Georgia O’Keeffe in 1938 to make paintings for a Dole campaign. She traveled to the Hawai‘i Territory in 1939,  painting valleys, flowers and the volcanic coast. She wanted to study pineapple plants where they grew, but company representatives would not allow her to stay among plantation workers. Back in Manhattan, still without a pineapple painting, she received a living plant sent by air cargo. She studied it in her apartment and painted Pineapple Bud (1939), later used in a Dole advertisement.
readmore: In January 1939, O’Keeffe left New York by train and crossed the continent before boarding the Lurline for Hawai‘i. At sea she wrote, “There is nothing in sight but the vibrating thing I am on…”
During nine weeks on the islands, she painted flowers, valleys and the volcanic coast. Some of these subjects interested her beyond the advertising assignment.
Back in Manhattan, she painted the pineapple plant sent to her by Dole. Pineapple Bud appeared in a November 1940 advertisement beside a family drinking pineapple juice.
At An American Place that year, she exhibited paintings drawn from her Hawaiian journey, some completed in New York from drawings, memories and objects she had brought home.

name: Museum of Modern Art — A Career On The Walls
intro: On May 14, 1946, the Museum of Modern Art opened a retrospective of Georgia O’Keeffe’s work—the first retrospective the museum had devoted to a woman artist. Charcoal drawings, flowers, skyscrapers and western landscapes occupied its galleries. O’Keeffe and Alfred Stieglitz saw the exhibition together. Thirty years earlier he had shown her charcoal drawings at 291, without asking her permission. Now a major New York museum displayed paintings and drawings made over decades, only weeks before Stieglitz’s death.
readmore: The exhibition was the result of months of practical work. O’Keeffe remembered packing large numbers of canvases. Photographer Todd Webb, recalling the preparations in 1991, described how carefully she expected every canvas to be handled:
“It was fun until [the photography curator] picked up one of the paintings wrong and Georgia blew up.”  “O’Keefe is a pretty good slave driver, and you had better be careful how you handle her work.”
MoMA’s account quoted her description of painting as a way to express “things I had no words for.”

The Museum of Modern Art had shown another side of O’Keeffe’s Manhattan work in 1932, when she submitted Manhattan, the central panel of a proposed mural triptych. By 1946 its rooms surveyed her abstractions, flowers, buildings and New Mexico subjects together.
After Stieglitz died, O’Keeffe helped organize the 1947 MoMA exhibition of his collection. The museum is still on West 53rd Street, though its galleries have been extensively changed.
Only a year later, O’Keeffe returned to help organize an exhibition of Stieglitz’s collection after his death.

name: Elizabeth Arden / Gymnasium Moderne
address: 691 Fifth Avenue at East 54th Street, New York, NY
intro: In 1936 Elizabeth Arden commissioned Georgia O’Keeffe to paint a monumental Jimson Weed for the Gymnasium Moderne at 689–691 Fifth Avenue. The canvas, nearly seven feet across, showed four luminous white flowers. Arden offered $10,000—far more than the $1,500 proposed for O’Keeffe’s unfinished Radio City Music Hall mural. O’Keeffe had obtained the new commission without Stieglitz’s help. Writing to their friend Henwar Rodakiewicz, she summed up the achievement in three words: “Got it myself.”
readmore: Arden’s Gymnasium Moderne occupied the Aeolian Building at Fifth Avenue and East 54th Street. It combined exercise, beauty treatments and fashionable social life. O’Keeffe’s enormous flower painting was made for that commercial interior, not for a conventional gallery wall.

Arden invited O’Keeffe into her social circle. Before attending one party, O’Keeffe sought support from critic Ralph Flint, telling him, “I’m only staying five minutes, I need support.” She remained for an hour and a half. A 1937 “Town & Country” feature photographed the Gymnasium Moderne and the work displayed there.

In 1938, Steuben commissioned another interpretation of her jimson weed design, this time for engraved glass. The flower that had filled Arden’s enormous canvas became an intimate object intended to be seen at close range.

name: 59 East 54th Street — Their Last Shared Apartment
intro: In December 1942, Georgia O’Keeffe and Alfred Stieglitz moved into 59 East 54th Street, their last shared apartment in Manhattan. The rooms were smaller than the Arno penthouse but closer to An American Place, Stieglitz’s gallery on Madison Avenue. O’Keeffe wrote to a friend about the change: “He is pleased with the change. I am not so pleased but I don’t really care.” While he remained close to his New York gallery, she spent increasingly long periods painting in New Mexico.
readmore: The couple’s lives were now divided between two places. Stieglitz continued to hang exhibitions and receive visitors at An American Place. O’Keeffe painted bones, adobe buildings and open country in New Mexico, returning to New York while maintaining their correspondence.  As O’Keeffe watched Stieglitz grow older, she wrote to a friend:  “I see Alfred as an old man that I am very fond of, growing older – so that sometimes it shocks and startles me when he looks particularly pale and tired – Aside from my fondness for him personally I feel that he has been very important to something that has made my world for me.”

In December 1945, O’Keeffe bought an abandoned adobe property at Abiquiú. Maria Chabot began restoring its walls, water supply and garden. A house suited to O’Keeffe’s work was taking shape far from their last shared Manhattan rooms. Stieglitz remained in New York until his death in July 1946.

name: Shelton Hotel
address: 525 Lexington Avenue (east side of Lexington Avenue at East 49th Street), New York, NY 10017
intro: Georgia O’Keeffe and Alfred Stieglitz moved into the Shelton Hotel in November 1925, first living on the twelfth floor and later on the thirtieth.
“I had never lived up so high before,” O’Keeffe recalled.
From the windows she saw rooftops, water towers, smoke and the East River. The young woman who had first learned Manhattan on foot was now painting it from above.
readmore: By 1928, O’Keeffe could afford the rooms that had once seemed beyond her means. She told a newspaper interviewer:
“When I came to live at the Shelton about three years ago … I couldn’t afford it. But I can now, so of course I’m going to stay.”
Journalist Frances O’Brien visited her in 1927 and described her working beside a large, carefully cleaned glass palette. As daylight faded and the telephone rang, O’Keeffe asked:
“Would you mind calling up a little later after the light goes?”

Stieglitz photographed the rooftops and river while O’Keeffe reorganized the same views into larger shapes of color. She also painted the Shelton itself, describing the sunlight in The Shelton with Sunspots, N.Y. as “a bite out of one side of the tower.”
The hotel was both their home and their workplace. In later years, it also became a place of growing tension in their marriage.

intro_html: Georgia O’Keeffe and Alfred Stieglitz moved into the Shelton Hotel in November 1925, first living on the twelfth floor and later on the thirtieth.
“I had never lived up so high before,” O’Keeffe recalled.
From the windows she saw rooftops, water towers, smoke and the East River. The young woman who had first learned Manhattan on foot was now painting it from above.
readmore_html: By 1928, O’Keeffe could afford the rooms that had once seemed beyond her means. She told a newspaper interviewer:
“When I came to live at the Shelton about three years ago … I couldn’t afford it. But I can now, so of course I’m going to stay.”
Journalist Frances O’Brien visited her in 1927 and described her working beside a large, carefully cleaned glass palette. As daylight faded and the telephone rang, O’Keeffe asked:
“Would you mind calling up a little later after the light goes?”

Stieglitz photographed the rooftops and river while O’Keeffe reorganized the same views into larger shapes of color. She also painted the Shelton itself, describing the sunlight in The Shelton with Sunspots, N.Y. as “a bite out of one side of the tower.”
The hotel was both their home and their workplace. In later years, it also became a place of growing tension in their marriage.

name: Arno Penthouse — A Larger Place To Work
intro: In April 1936, Georgia O’Keeffe and Alfred Stieglitz left the Shelton for a penthouse at the Arno, 405 East 54th Street. O’Keeffe wanted space to make larger paintings. Bright rooms faced the East River and Welfare Island, while a terrace opened to the skyline. Inside, striped Navajo rugs crossed dark floors; shells and other objects from the Southwest shared her rooms with New York views. The lease and telephone were in her name, and she paid the household bills.
readmore: Stieglitz resisted leaving the Shelton, according to O’Keeffe’s biographers. In their new apartment at the Arno, he left his trunk unpacked for months. With three bedrooms, the apartment offered a different kind of domestic space from the room they had shared at the Shelton.

A 1937 photograph by Kurt Severin shows O’Keeffe arranging shells in the sunlit apartment. In another period photograph she placed a bleached skull from New Mexico against a brick wall on the terrace, the Manhattan skyline beyond it. Her objects and pictures made the Southwest present inside her city home.
The address survives at 405 East 54th Street.
Stieglitz continued inviting friends to Saturday dinners. A cook-housekeeper prepared the meals, while O’Keeffe sometimes sat apart sewing.
The apartment was large enough for their lives to take different shapes within the same rooms.

name: An American Place
address: 509 Madison Avenue, Room 1710, New York, NY
intro: On December 15, 1929, Alfred Stieglitz opened An American Place in six pearl-gray rooms on the seventeenth floor of 509 Madison Avenue.
Here he exhibited O’Keeffe’s paintings of New York, Lake George and New Mexico. Her travels increasingly took her away from Manhattan, but her paintings returned to these rooms.
readmore: Stieglitz did not offer elaborate invitations, cocktail parties or press previews. He wanted visitors to come and look.
During O’Keeffe’s first extended stay in New Mexico in 1929, he wrote, “Fill yourself to the fullest.” He ended the letter by calling her “my wild Georgia O’Keeffe.”
Yet their attachments to different places were becoming increasingly apparent. O’Keeffe later explained: “He was a city man and I was a country person.”
In October 1950, four years after Stieglitz’s death, O’Keeffe returned to install the gallery’s final exhibition. As at 291 in 1917, the last paintings on its walls were hers.

name: Anderson Galleries / Intimate Gallery
address: Historic 489 Park Avenue near East 59th Street, New York, NY
intro: In February 1921, Alfred Stieglitz exhibited 145 photographs at the Anderson Galleries, 489 Park Avenue. Forty-five were studies of Georgia O’Keeffe—her face, hands, posture and, in some photographs, her nude body. He called the sequence a Demonstration of Portraiture. In January 1923, the same galleries opened One Hundred Pictures by O’Keeffe, showing her own art on a much larger scale. Stieglitz opened the Intimate Gallery in the building in December 1925, continuing his exhibition program.
readmore: In 1921, Stieglitz exhibited forty-five photographs of O’Keeffe as part of his larger photographic exhibition. The portraits made her known to people who scarcely knew her paintings.
Two years later, her own exhibition filled the galleries. She explained what painting had made possible:
“I found that I could say things with color and shapes that I couldn’t say in any other way — things that I had no words for.”
She was also candid about the practical realities of being an artist. For her 1924 exhibition, she wrote:
“Incidentally I hope someone will buy something. I have kept my pictures small because space in New York necessitated that.”
In December 1925, Stieglitz opened the Intimate Gallery in the same building.

name: 51 East 60th Street — Anita Pollitzer’s network
intro: In March 1916 O’Keeffe returned to New York and enrolled in Arthur Wesley Dow's Teachers College course in teaching methods, a requirement connected with her forthcoming position at West Texas State Normal College in Canyon. She stayed with Anita Pollitzer's relatives at 51 East 60th Street.4

That January, Pollitzer had carried O’Keeffe’s abstract charcoal drawings to Alfred Stieglitz at 291. Only weeks later, in May, O’Keeffe discovered that Stieglitz had placed ten of her drawings on public exhibition without asking her.
readmore: Anita Pollitzer had recognized something original in O’Keeffe’s charcoal drawings and carried them to Stieglitz in January 1916.
O’Keeffe wanted to know what he had seen in them. To Pollitzer, whose friendship had opened this unexpected door, she wrote:
“There seems nothing for me to say except thank you – very calmly and quietly.”

name: 1111 Madison Avenue — Stieglitz Family Home
intro: Before Georgia O’Keeffe entered Alfred Stieglitz’s life, 1111 Madison Avenue was where he resided with his wife Emmeline and daughter Kitty. In 1918, after O’Keeffe returned to New York, he brought her to the apartment to photograph her while his wife was away. Emmeline came home unexpectedly. Soon afterward Stieglitz moved out and joined O’Keeffe in the borrowed studio at 114 East 59th Street.
readmore: Stieglitz had married Emmeline Obermeyer in 1893. Her family’s brewing-related wealth helped support his photographic work and his efforts to exhibit modern art. His photographs from 1111 Madison Avenue also show that the apartment was a place from which he observed the city.

After the confrontation in 1918, he wrote to his secretary, “I’m out of 1111 – In one hour and fifty minutes the job was completed – You never saw such a clean job and the place was left spic and span.  Mrs. wasn’t home.  So, she probably had a great surprise when she turned up.  She probably had no idea anyone could act so promptly and quickly…  I’m really very sorry for Mrs. S…But what can I do?  I was certainly patient and persistent.”
Thirteen years later, the situation was reversed. O’Keeffe returned unexpectedly to their Shelton apartment and discovered Stieglitz with Dorothy Norman.

name: 60 East 65th Street — Leopold Stieglitz’s Home
intro: In December 1920, Georgia O’Keeffe and Alfred Stieglitz moved into the home of Stieglitz’s brother Leopold at 60 East 65th Street. They spent New York winters there through 1924. name: Plaza Hotel and South Central Park
intro: During her first New York year, Georgia O’Keeffe walked the mile from her lodging at the Eva Home on East 62nd Street toward the Art Students League on West 57th Street, often passing through Central Park. She later remembered walking past the Plaza Hotel, into the park and then turning toward the school.
readmore: Recounting her early routine in “My First Trip to New York,” a 95-year-old O’Keeffe wrote that she “walked to the lower end of central park – past the Plaza [hotel] – till I turned to go to the school building.” She added, “I hardly ever met anyone going through the park.”

The Plaza opened in 1907 at Fifth Avenue and Central Park South. It survives as an easily recognizable point on the route between the Upper East Side and the Art Students League. The historical postcard shows the hotel in the period O’Keeffe first knew Manhattan.

name: Art Students League
intro: Georgia O’Keeffe studied at the Art Students League at 215 West 57th Street in 1907–1908. Fellow student Eugene Speicher repeatedly asked her to pose for him.
“Speicher wanted to paint me—but I wanted to work myself,” she remembered.
She eventually sat for his portrait, but it was a prize awarded to her own painting, Dead Rabbit with Copper Pot, that took her to the League’s summer school at Lake George.
readmore: Speicher had told her that he would become a great painter while she would probably end up teaching painting in a girls’ school.

Forty years later, in December 1948, LIFE magazine published a photograph of O’Keeffe standing beside his portrait of her. By then she had received a major retrospective at the Museum of Modern Art and become one of America’s most celebrated artists.
The photograph brought the beginning of her New York life face to face with its approaching end.

intro_html: In 1912, while studying with Alon Bement in Virginia, O’Keeffe encountered the compositional ideas of Arthur Wesley Dow. In autumn 1914 she came to Teachers College at Columbia University to study in Dow’s orbit, returning again in spring 1916.
Dow’s approach offered a way to organize pictures through line, mass and rhythm rather than simply copying appearances.

She later identified No. 14 Special (1916) as the drawing she made during that exercise.

name: Mount Sinai Hospital — A Skylight Remembered
intro: In 1927 Georgia O’Keeffe underwent two operations at Mount Sinai Hospital for benign breast cysts. She later recalled the bright skylight above her as an anesthetic took hold. The opening seemed to spin and become a “small white dot in the black room.” Within weeks she painted Black Abstraction (1927), a composition of darkness around a tiny point of light. A 1922 photograph documents a similar skylit operating room at the hospital.
readmore: In her much later account, O’Keeffe remembered looking up at “a very large bright skylight above me.” As the anesthetic took effect, the light seemed to contract until only a dot remained. The experience offered her a subject that she translated into an abstract painting.
The selected period photograph of Mount Sinai’s Operating Room 7 shows a skylight similar to what she described.
The selected 1922 operating-room photograph provides historical context and has not been identified as the room in which O’Keeffe underwent surgery.

name: Doctors Hospital — Illness and Farewell
address: 170 East End Avenue, New York, NY
intro: In February 1933, after the collapse of her Radio City Music Hall commission and during a period of severe personal strain, Georgia O’Keeffe entered Doctors Hospital at 170 East End Avenue.
She would return to the same hospital thirteen years later, when Alfred Stieglitz was dying.
readmore: By the end of 1932, O’Keeffe had stopped painting. In a Christmas greeting to Henwar Rodakiewicz, she described herself as “absurdly ill with a crazy heart.”
After leaving Doctors Hospital, she continued recovering in Bermuda. By late 1933 she was drawing again, and in January 1934 she returned to painting.
Her recovery was not without uncertainty. In February she wrote to Rodakiewicz:
“I get long periods of uncertainties in my mind and I do not like to write them to any one.”
In July 1946, O’Keeffe was working in New Mexico when word reached her that Stieglitz had suffered a stroke. She hurried east. He died at Doctors Hospital on July 13.
The hospital that had been part of her recovery became the place where their life together ended.

name: Whitney Museum — 1970 Retrospective
address: 945 Madison Avenue at East 75th Street, New York, NY
intro: In October 1970, the Whitney Museum of American Art opened a major retrospective of Georgia O’Keeffe at its then-new Madison Avenue building. O’Keeffe came to New York to help install the exhibition. More than six decades had passed since she attended the Art Students League and made her first Manhattan drawings. The paintings brought together in the Whitney’s galleries came from many years and places, including the city she had painted from the Shelton Hotel. She helped shape their presentation herself.
readmore: The 1970 retrospective took place at 945 Madison Avenue, in the building that now occupies the museum’s former Upper East Side site.
The Whitney now operates at 99 Gansevoort Street.
O’Keeffe had come to Manhattan in 1907 as an unknown student. More than six decades later, she returned to help install an exhibition surveying her own life’s work.

name: Brooklyn Bridge — A Late New York Subject
intro: In 1949 Georgia O’Keeffe studied the Brooklyn Bridge by car on Sunday mornings, driving through lower Manhattan and back and forth across the East River. She turned its towers and suspension cables into the painting Brooklyn Bridge (1949), simplifying the crossing into broad stone masses, vertical lines and openings of sky. She made New Mexico her permanent home that June.
readmore: In the finished painting, O’Keeffe removed most of the surrounding city and reduced the structure to stone masses, verticals, curves and openings of sky.

Four decades earlier, her carefully observed still life Dead Rabbit with Copper Pot had won a prize at the Art Students League. Now she could take one of New York’s most recognizable structures and transform it through selection and simplification.

name: 35 East 58th Street — First Married-Period Home
intro: In November 1924, Georgia O’Keeffe and Alfred Stieglitz moved into an apartment at 35 East 58th Street. His divorce from Emmeline had become final in September. They married on December 11 at the home of their friend John Marin in Cliffside Park, New Jersey, and returned to their Manhattan apartment without a reception or honeymoon. Their first married-period home lasted only about a year. In November 1925 they moved to the Shelton Hotel and began a different chapter of city life.
readmore: O’Keeffe and Stieglitz had lived together for six years before marrying. She later recalled that she had not wanted the wedding. There was no reception or honeymoon; they returned to their Manhattan apartment.
Marriage did not change the name by which she wanted to be known:
“So when people would say ‘Mrs. Stieglitz,’ I would say ‘Miss O’Keeffe.’”
Their first married-period home lasted about a year before they moved to the Shelton Hotel.

name: 114 East 59th Street — the 59th Street Studio
intro: In June 1918, Georgia O’Keeffe left her Texas teaching job and moved to a studio at 114 East 59th Street lent by Alfred Stieglitz’s niece Elizabeth. Stieglitz joined her in July and began photographing her. O’Keeffe remembered a bright front room with a north skylight and south-facing windows, followed by a much darker room beyond a narrow opening. In 59th St. Studio (1919), she painted that passage from light to shadow. The rooms gave her time to paint without a teaching schedule.
Eleven years earlier, O’Keeffe had arrived in New York by boat, looking for a brother who failed to meet her. When she returned in June 1918, Stieglitz was waiting at Pennsylvania Station.
He had offered to support a year devoted to her painting. Accepting meant leaving the teaching salary that had sustained her.
readmore: Stieglitz had offered to support a year devoted to her painting. At the studio, O’Keeffe found the combination of light, privacy and work time she had lacked while earning a teaching salary.

In the same rooms Stieglitz photographed her face, hands, shoulders, clothes and sometimes her unclothed body. Some portraits would be displayed publicly at the Anderson Galleries in 1921, changing how people knew both artists.
The later city tax photograph documents the exterior; the selected Sanborn map shows the old building layout and the north skylight captured by O’Keeffe in her painting.

name: Camera Club of New York — Before 291
intro: In 1897 Alfred Stieglitz became editor of Camera Notes, the journal of the Camera Club of New York. He filled its pages with carefully chosen photographs and criticism arguing that photography deserved recognition as an art. The work predated his acquaintance with Georgia O’Keeffe and even his gallery at 291. The historic Camera Club building associated with West 29th Street recalls the institutional world from which Stieglitz would eventually break to publish Camera Work and found the Photo-Secession.
readmore: Stieglitz had studied photographic science in Berlin before returning to New York. At the Camera Club he demanded high standards of photographic printing and reproduction. Disagreements with other members grew; in 1902 he resigned as editor of Camera Notes.
In 1903 he launched Camera Work, an independent journal containing closely supervised photogravures. Its fine printing was itself part of his argument that photographs could be works of art.
Stieglitz supervised finely graded photogravures, some printed on delicate Japanese tissue.

name: Madison Square Park — Stieglitz’s Flatiron
address: Madison Square Park / Flatiron District, New York, NY
intro: In the winter of 1903, Alfred Stieglitz photographed the Flatiron Building through the trees of Madison Square Park. He remembered the tower rising through the weather like the “bow of a monster ocean steamer.” In The Flatiron, dark branches partly screen the new skyscraper as it emerges through wintry haze. The photograph belongs to the Manhattan Stieglitz had learned to see before O’Keeffe arrived. Years later, she too would turn the city’s towers into carefully composed images.
readmore: Stieglitz was making a case for photography as an art in the same years he edited Camera Notes and established the Photo-Secession.

name: Metropolitan Museum of Art — Defending a Photograph
intro: After Alfred Stieglitz died in 1946, Georgia O’Keeffe worked with Doris Bry to sort and protect his photographs and extensive art collection. She examined prints, paper, mounts and their condition before arranging gifts to museums. At the Metropolitan Museum of Art, a curator proposed trimming mounts on some photographs to make them fit storage boxes. O’Keeffe refused. Rather than permit the photographs to be altered, she withdrew the proposed gift. The dispute shows how firmly she defended the choices Stieglitz had made when finishing his prints.
readmore: Stieglitz’s photographs were physical objects, not merely images. He had selected the paper, orientation, cropping and mounts. After his death, O’Keeffe treated those decisions as part of the finished work.

She and Bry reviewed thousands of photographs before deciding what could enter institutional collections. A large group reached the National Gallery of Art in 1949, with the portraits of O’Keeffe following a different schedule.
O’Keeffe regarded the paper, orientation, cropping and mounts as part of the finished photographs. Preserving Stieglitz’s work meant preserving those decisions as well as the images themselves.

name: Brooklyn Museum — First Museum Retrospective
intro: In June 1927, the Brooklyn Museum opened Paintings by Georgia O’Keeffe, presenting fifteen paintings through September 1. It was her first museum retrospective. Among the works was The Red Maple at Lake George (1926), listed as number one in the exhibition. For years Alfred Stieglitz had shown her paintings in his Manhattan galleries. Now a public museum was exhibiting them beyond his rooms.
readmore: The exhibition records show the practical work of borrowing, valuing, displaying and returning paintings. Fifteen works could be a small exhibition in number yet a significant step for an artist already widely discussed in Stieglitz’s circle.
The Brooklyn Museum today owns O’Keeffe’s Brooklyn Bridge (1949) and a preparatory study.

Nine years after returning to New York to devote herself to painting, O’Keeffe had a museum exhibition of her own. The Brooklyn Museum would eventually also hold one of her last major New York subjects, Brooklyn Bridge (1949).
